messages.author: b8c77fa5305c80cb
messages.subject: Improving performance
parts:
I have a very large data.frame
The data.frame contains ~800 rows and ~10K columns.

I have a vector of functions which performs a cleaning, an example of such a function is:
ret_func <- function (features_list) {
        features_list[["f1]][features_list$NPACKETS_DIR_0 + features_list$NPACKETS_DIR_1 < num_packets] = NA;
        return (features_list[["f1"]);
    }

I then called it by using:
res = data.frame(lapply(feature_structures,function(g,d) { g(d) }, features_list ),stringsAsFactors=F)

The problem with this is that it takes a really long time to calculate (Around 1 minute on my computer and I need to do this on lots of such data frames).

So I decided to use Rcpp.
What I did was change the function to look something like this:


void min_packet_i_clean_func_int(DataFrame DL, String feature_name,int num_packets)
{
    IntegerVector feature_vec = DL[feature_name];
    IntegerVector NPKTS_0 = DL["NPACKETS_DIR_0"];
    IntegerVector NPKTS_1 = DL["NPACKETS_DIR_1"];
    int n = feature_vec.size();
    for(int n_row = 0; n_row < n; n_row++) {
        int pkt = NPKTS_0[n_row] + NPKTS_1[n_row];
        }
        if(pkt < num_packets) {
            feature_vec[n_row] = NA_INTEGER;
        }
    }
}

and then call it using:
    for(f in feature_structures) {
        f(res_env);
    }

This improved the performance by a factor of almost 1000!
The problem is that i want the change to occur in place (i.e. don't copy the data but instead pass the data by reference and change it directly).
This works properly for integer rows but fails for non integer rows. For non integer rows it works by value (i.e. it makes the change but creates a new version of the data which is both not what I wanted and takes longer).
So I added a comperable function which is numeric based and one which is logical based. The problem is that I do not know how to check what type of row I am using.
I thought of doing something like: 
type=class(feature_list[[feature_name]])
func=switch(class,integer=func1, numerical=func2,logical=func3);
func(feature_list,feature_name,num_packets);

but that would mean doing a copy of the row. It is still a lot faster than before but it does have a cost.
I was wondering if there is a way to do this better (either to find the class of the vector.

Another problem that I saw is that if I do:
features_list2=feature_list
then call the function, both feature_lists change while if I do:
features_list2=feature_list
a=feature_list2[1,1];
feature_list2[1,1]=NA
feature_list2[1,1]=a
then only feature_list changes.
I assume this is because R performs a "copy on write" methodology, is there a better way to do this?

messages.subject: Re: [Israel RUG] Improving performance
parts:
I believe copy actually creates a new copy thereby not doing the whole "by reference" bit, I was looking for something which activates the copy on write bit.
In any case, following is what I did (this is of course slimmed down than the full code...):
in the cpp file:

#include <Rcpp.h>
using namespace Rcpp;

/// Function to clean up a column based on number of packets
///
/// This function recieves a data frame and changes a single column (feature) in it
/// in place (i.e. by reference). The change is to turn illegal values to NA.
/// Values would change to NA if there are not enough packets to reach 'i'.
/// @note The column @b MUST be an integer vector, otherwise it might be copied instead
///       both wasting memory and losing the information when the function exists
/// @param DL The data frame to change
/// @param feature_name The name of the feature (column) we are currently fixing
/// @param i We need at least this number of packets to have arrived for the data to be valid.
void clean_int(DataFrame DL, String feature_name,int i)

{
    IntegerVector feature_vec = DL[feature_name];
IntegerVector NPKTS = DL["NPACKETS"];

int n = feature_vec.size();
    for(int n_row = 0; n_row < n; n_row++) {

if(NPKTS[n_row] < i) {
            feature_vec[n_row] = NA_INTEGER;
        }
    }
}

/// Function to clean up a column based on number of packets
///
/// This function recieves a data frame and changes a single column (feature) in it
/// in place (i.e. by reference). The change is to turn illegal values to NA.
/// Values would change to NA if there are not enough packets to reach 'i'.
/// @note The column @b MUST be a numeric vector, otherwise it might be copied instead
///       both wasting memory and losing the information when the function exists
/// @param DL The data frame to change
/// @param feature_name The name of the feature (column) we are currently fixing
/// @param i We need at least this number of packets to have arrived for the data to be valid.
void clean_numeric(DataFrame DL, String feature_name,int i)
{
    NumericVector feature_vec = DL[feature_name];
    IntegerVector NPKTS = DL["NPACKETS"];

int n = feature_vec.size();
    for(int n_row = 0; n_row < n; n_row++) {

if(NPKTS[n_row] < i) {
            feature_vec[n_row] = NA_REAL;
        }
    }
}


/// Function to clean up a column based on number of packets
///
/// This function recieves a data frame and changes a single column (feature) in it
/// in place (i.e. by reference). The change is to turn illegal values to NA.
/// Values would change to NA if there are not enough packets to reach 'i'.
/// @param DL The data frame to change
/// @param feature_name The name of the feature (column) we are currently fixing
/// @param i We need at least this number of packets to have arrived for the data to be valid.
// [[Rcpp::export]]
void clean_func(DataFrame DL, String feature_name,int i)
{
    switch(TYPEOF(DL[feature_name])) {
        case REALSXP:
            clean_numeric(DL,feature_name,i);
            break;
        case INTSXP:
            clean_int(DL,feature_name,i);
            break;
        default:
            stop("Only integer and numeric vectors are supported");
        break;
           
    }
}

In R:
I sourced the cpp file and defined the cleaning function as such:

# A generation function (it creates the actual function)
# the generated function will have the data be legal if at least 'i' packets arrived.
# input: feature_name: A string containing the feature name
# Input: 'i' the number of packets which should arrive for the data to be legal
# Output: A cleaning function.
generate_min_packet_i_clean_func <- function(feature_name,i) { 
    # input: features_list: the environment containing the feature list data frame
    # return: The specific feature vector with all values where packet number is smaller than or equal to
    # i+1 are set to NA
    ret_func <- function(feature_list_ptr) {
        clean_func(feature_list_ptr$value, feature_name, i);
    }
    return (ret_func);
}


The generation function is called on the features with some logic. I then have a vector containing the resulting features.

I then do the cleaning as such:
# function to apply cleaning functions on the data frame
# input: feature_list A data.frame containing the data. It must include the NPACKETS column
# input: feature_structures A vector containing the cleaning function
# return: A cleaned version of the data frame
clean_features <- function(features_list, feature_structures) {
    # make the call to the function "by reference" by passing it through an environment.
    res_env = new.env();
    res_env$value = features_list;
    # the following lines handle the fact that R uses lazy copy on write, this forces
    # the data to be copied for the first time to avoid changing the source.
    a = res_env$value[1,1];
    res_env$value[1,1] = NA;
    res_env$value[1,1] = a;
   
    # go over the functions one by one.
    for(f in feature_structures) {
        f(res_env);
    }
    #extract the result, apply the filter and return the result.
    res = res_env$value;
    rm(res_env);
    return (res);   
}

btw, originally The cleaning function looked like this:
generate_min_packet_i_clean_func <- function(feature_name,i) { 
    ret_func <- function(feature_list) {
        feature_list[[feature_name]][feature_list[["NPACKETS"]]<=i] = NA;
    }
    return (ret_func);
}

and it was called by:
res = data.frame(lapply(feature_structures,function(g,d) { g(d) }, features_list ),stringsAsFactors=F)

The difference in performance was more than 1000 times faster!!!
In general the move to "by reference" to the function improved around 15-20% while the move to cpp did the rest...
